items.title: 가평 단독주택 화재로 50대 남녀 2명 숨져…1명 화상
items.summary: 31일 오전 0시 38분께 경기 가평군 조종면 신하리의 한 단독주택에서 불이 나 50대 남녀 2명이 숨졌다.“50대 아내와 남동생이 집 안에 남아 있다”는 신고를 받은 소방 당국은 인력 58명과 장비 24대를 투입해 진화에 나섰다.구조대는 오전 1시 23분께 건물 안쪽 방에서 심정지 상태인 2명을 발견해 병원으로 옮겼으나 숨졌다.함께 있던 3명은 대피했으며, 이 중 50대 남성 1명은 손에 2도 화상을 입어 병원 치료를 받았다.불은 샌드위치 패널로 된 주택과 인접한 간이 찜질방을 태운 뒤 오전 2시 24분께 완전히 꺼졌다.경찰과 소방 당국은 LPG 난로에서 가스가 새 불이 났을 가능성 등 화재 원인을 조사 중이다. 오는 11월 2일 합동 감식도 진행할 예정이다.(가평=뉴스1)

items.title: 전 연인에 “불 지르겠다” 협박한 20대 구속영장 기각
items.summary: 헤어진 연인의 집을 찾아가 자신의 몸에 인화성 물질을 뿌리고 불을 지르겠다며 협박한 혐의를 받는 20대 여성이 구속을 면했다. 서울남부지법 박찬석 부장판사는 31일 오후 3시 스토킹처벌법 위반, 특수협박, 주거침입, 현주건조물방화예비 혐의를 받는 20대 여성 권씨에 대한 구속 전 피의자 심문(영장실질심사)을 연 후 구속영장을 기각했다. 박 부장판사는 “범행에 이른 경위와 잠정조치 전후 피해자의 태도, 둘 사이의 교류의 경과, 범행의 구체적인 내용과 피해 정도 등을 종합하면 현 단계에서 재범하거나 도주 또는 증거를 인멸할 우려가 없다”고 기각 사유를 밝혔다.권씨는 지난 29일 오후 7시20분께 서울 구로구에 있는 전 연인 20대 남성 A씨 집을 찾아가 자신의 몸에 인화성 물질을 뿌리고 협박한 혐의를 받는다.권씨는 지난 26일부터 일본 여행 중이던 A씨의 지인들에게 반복적으로 연락했고, 이를 알게 된 A씨가 경찰에 스토킹 신고를 한 것으로 파악됐다.이후 경찰은 지난 28일 추가

items.title: 진주 송전탑서 작업하던 60대, 20m 아래 추락해 숨져
items.summary: 경남 진주에서 송전탑 전선교체 작업을 하던 60대 근로자가 추락해 숨졌다. 31일 소방 등에 따르면 이날 오후 5시 5분경 진주시 가좌동의 한 송전탑에서 작업을 하던 60대 근로자가 20m 아래로 추락했다. 이 사고로 머리 등을 크게 다친 근로자는 심정지 상태로 병원으로 이송됐지만 사망했다. 경찰 조사 결과, 이날 오전 7시부터 사고가 난 송전탑 위에서 근로자 3명이 전선 교체작업을 하고 있었다. 경찰은 정확한 사고 경위와 함께 안전관리 책임자를 상대로 안전수칙 준수 등 업무상과실 여부도 조사 중이다.

items.title: 거제 공사 현장서 전신주 파손…1200세대 아파트 단지 정전
items.summary: 경남 거제시 아주동 한 공사장서 31일, 전신주가 파손돼 인근 아파트 단지 1200여세대가 한때 정전됐다.한국전력공사 경남본부에 따르면 이날 오후 2시 15분께 거제시 아주동 내곡지구 한 공사장에서 전신주가 파손돼 인근 아파트 1200세대에 전기 공급이 끊겨 주민들이 불편을 겪었다.한전은 임시 복구 작업을 벌여, 정전 발생 후 약 35분 만에 전기 공급을 재개했다.거제시는 내곡지구 공사 현장에서 전신주를 건드려 정전이 발생한 것으로 확인하고. 이날 오후 4시께 안전안내 문자를 보내 “도로 통제로 아주동 버스정류장의 버스 운행이 중단된다”며 “차량은 우회해 달라”고 당부했다. 한전은 파손된 전신주를 교체하는 한편 주변 도로를 통제했다.[거제=뉴시스]

items.title: The Guardian view on 50 years of The Selfish Gene: flawed, outdated, yet still a model of truly popular science writing | Editorial
items.summary: Richard Dawkins’ first work has thrilled fans and frustrated critics for five decades. The science has moved on, but any writer looking to supplant its place must learn its lessons Richard Dawkins’ The Selfish Gene was not predicted to be a success. Its initial print run, published this week in 1976, was just 5,000. It went on to sell millions, and is perhaps the most influential work of pop-science ever. For 50 years, it has been the go-to resource for the layperson seeking to understand evolution. What accounts for its enduring power? Prof Dawkins’ central claim, that “we are survival machines – robot vehicles blindly programmed to preserve the selfish molecules known as genes” was provocative, stripping the messy stuff of human and other life down to a simple law. And yet the book is primarily concerned with proving that complex, selfless behaviour such as altruism in animals can emerge from these basic “selfish” drives, satisfyingly resolving an apparent paradox. Prof Dawkins – a zoologist by training – also succeeded in conjuring entertaining, vividly drawn vignettes of the lives of animals, from lions and ants to hawks and honeybees, to make his points. articles.title: Jump scares, leather gloves and squeaking moth noises: theatre horror masters on how they make their shows so scary
articles.snippet: Whether it’s immersive chiller Blackout or the campily scary 2:22: A Ghost Story, ‘tis the season to be scared witless at the theatre. But what’s the secret to making an audience gasp in terror? It was 1am. Total darkness. Locking up a wedding venue, Sam Beech’s car sensor went off: there was something behind him. “It went on for half an hour,” the writer and director recalls, “on the front bumper, then round the back. But every time I looked, there was nothing.” It kept going, snuffling around the car. So he stopped looking. “I thought: ‘If I don’t look behind me, it won’t get me.’” Since then, Beech, the creator of one of a plethora of horror shows currently haunting the stage, admits, “I don’t like driving in the dark”. Beech’s experience was eerily similar to a scene in Andy Nyman’s hit 2010 play Ghost Stories, which Beech had seen four times, so the gnarly end the character had met on stage filled his mind when the sensor went off in the dark. Now, the uncanny experience has fed into his own new horror show Blackout (touring the UK to 27 February), which uses everything that made him so scared that night: the quiet, the absence, the idea of something lurking in the shadows. “It’s the Jaws effect,” says Chris Fisher, the illusions designer behind the stage show of Paranormal Activity (at London Ambassador’s theatre to 27 February, and touring the UK), which had me sheepishly checking under my bed for several nights and stopped just short of nightmares. “It’s scarier to see the fin and hear the music,” Fisher says, “than it is to see the mechanical head of the shark.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Dónal Lunny obituary
articles.snippet: Producer and musician who played with the influential Irish folk bands Planxty, the Bothy Band and Moving Hearts Dónal Lunny, who has died of cancer aged 79, was a multi-instrumentalist in three of the most influential folk bands of the late 20th century: Planxty, the Bothy Band and Moving Hearts. He played the guitar, keyboards and bodhrán, but he is best remembered for popularising the bouzouki in Irish traditional music. The round-bodied bouzouki from Greece was adapted by Lunny, resulting in a flat-backed instrument with a shorter neck known as the Irish bouzouki. Lunny often worked in collaboration with the singer and songwriter Christy Moore and the musician Andy Irvine. In all the bands with which he was associated, Lunny played a vital role in arranging the music, being instinctively drawn to developing new harmonic and rhythmic structures. He produced many Irish music albums, also working with artists including Elvis Costello, Kate Bush, Sinéad O’Connor and Mark Knopfler. As a composer, he wrote and arranged the music for films, documentaries and television programmes. In 1991, he was the musical director of the joint BBC and RTÉ television series Bringing It All Back Home, which won an Emmy. Continue reading...

articles.title: Oh to Believe in Another World review – William Kentridge’s amazing animated ballet of black comic pain
articles.snippet: Kentridge’s cine-musical creation, made to accompany Shostakovich’s 10th Symphony, is a marvel of puppetry, dance and humour, exploring humanity, grief and idealism The Baku international arts festival in Azerbaijan is showcasing an amazing cine-musical creation, perhaps the most amazing animation I have ever seen. Oh to Believe in Another World is an hour-long collage animation with live-action choreography by the 71-year-old South African artist and film-maker William Kentridge. It is shown with the live orchestral accompaniment of Shostakovich’s 10th Symphony, and this event is partly in honour of the 120th anniversary of Shostakovich’s birth this year, and partly to honour Shostakovich’s reportedly unrequited love (and lifelong friendship) for his student, Azerbaijani pianist and composer Elmira Nazirova. The 10th symphony was inspired by Stalin and premiered shortly after his death, so it seems probable that Shostakovich had been at work on it for some time before this, long enough beforehand for at least some of the composition to have been conceived without any sense of Stalin’s death. Could part of it perhaps have been originally intended as an obediently dramatic tribute to Stalin? Yet the music arguably combines fear, awe, revulsion, and a hysterical reaction to the mad energy of Stalin’s genocidal tyranny, a darkly ambiguous respect for the great dictator whose victory in 1945 was a mainstay of the postwar dispensation; perhaps there is also a feeling in the music’s swirl that a great and terrible era has passed away, and with it a kind of grief at all that had been sacrificed to it. articles.title: The real problem with Britain’s Political Traitors show is that no one is very faithful to anything for long | Robert Hutton
articles.snippet: For Westminster’s special budget edition of the series, politicians have played to their strengths. Bombast, duplicity, distrust: it’s all second nature You join us on a steam train in Scotland as we head to the next episode of the BBC’s hit show Political Traitors. It’s like the celebrity edition, except that everyone is less comely – politics being the practice of show business for ugly people. For this week’s task, the players have to construct a “budget” of tiny crowd-pleasing measures, carefully balanced by invisible tax rises. What makes the show so compelling is that the players don’t know the whole story. Only those of us on the outside can see what’s really going on. articles.title: The Guardian view on Labour’s fiscal devolution: the future of Burnhamism will play out in municipal England | Editorial
articles.snippet: Replacing government grants with revenue streams from taxation will not in itself reduce regional inequalities. But the political implications are radical Following Wednesday’s budget, the Treasury minister, Torsten Bell, was challenged by the BBC’s Evan Davis on whether its modest series of “breathing space” measures could truly be said to have ended “40 years of neoliberalism”. This line of questioning is becoming a familiar one. Andy Burnham’s ringing declaration of long-term intent is now being regularly deployed by commentators to suggest an emerging gulf between rhetoric and action. Mr Bell’s response was a good one. Recalling how “Margaret Thatcher in the 1980s hugely hollowed out local government [and] tried to emasculate our big cities”, he called the fiscal devolution roadmap unveiled in the budget a step change and a really big deal.From 2028, mayoral strategic authorities will for the first time receive a share of income tax receipts, and from next year they will be allocated 20% of business rates revenue. That figure will potentially rise to 100% by the end of the decade, while a new overnight visitors levy will add another local income stream.
